source.title: Secret mixtures of experts inside your LLM

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses dictionary-sparse inputs and an approximately orthogonal dictionary as assumptions in its theoretical account, but its experiments test whether MLP layers can be distilled into sparse MoEs, not whether superposition or any listed version holds.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior observations of dictionary-sparse activations and prior arguments linking approximate orthogonality to superposition; these are not its own results. Its conditional theorems assume dictionary sparsity and approximate orthogonality rather than measuring them. The distillation results concern sparse-MoE approximability, which none of the claim versions directly names, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Learning-rate choices and the shared-expert and router ablations are not results about the claim's feature representation.
record.test_reason: The paper takes dictionary sparsity of activations (citing Bricken et al.) and approximately orthogonal dictionaries (citing Toy Models) as premises for its theorems. Its experiments measure only how well sparse-MoE versus dense-MLP students distil one MLP layer. No feature geometry, polysemanticity, SAE recovery, or feature dimensionality is measured. The activation-versus-Gaussian contrast shows the activation distribution has non-Gaussian structure that MoEs exploit. That structure is not shown to be sparse features or superposition, so it is a related construct and goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also prove two theorems as motivation. First, under isotropic Gaussian inputs, sparse MoEs cannot approximate even the identity. Second, under dictionary-sparse inputs with an approximately orthogonal dictionary, sparse MoEs can approximate linear functions and low-rank-interaction polynomials. They present the distillation results as validating that dense MLPs secretly compute sparse MoE-like functions, explaining MoE effectiveness. They also suggest low-rank routers as a design direction.
record.recipe_differences: The paper distills pretrained transformer MLP layers into sparse MoE students and compares them with MLP students; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition experiments or their feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs between activation data and matched-mean-and-covariance Gaussian data. The paper also reports that low-rank routing generally improves distillation on activation data, but that is an architecture ablation rather than a measurement of the claim's feature geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: On activation data, sparse-MoE students (single-neuron experts plus a shared expert, low-rank router) explain more variance of middle MLP layers than same-active-neuron MLP students. This holds for Pythia-70m, Gemma-3-270m and Pythia-410m, with up to roughly 8x fewer active neurons in some cases. The advantage largely vanishes on Gaussian inputs with matched mean and covariance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dense MLP layers in pretrained LLMs are well approximated by sparsely-activating MoEs under their own activation distribution, and this depends on non-Gaussian (hypothesised dictionary-sparse) input structure.

record.problems: The claim-relevant feature geometry is not directly measured. Main comparisons are presented in plots without exact values in the text; uncertainty estimates and repeated-run variability are not stated. The experiments cover only one middle layer in each of three pretrained models.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-related rows omitted. Shared-expert and routing ablations (Table 1 and Figure 6), and learning-rate loss curves (Figures 7–12), concern distillation design rather than the listed feature-representation versions.

untested.parts: No toy-model experiments; sparsity transition and geometry not measured.
Capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features not examined.
Origins of polysemantic neurons not examined.
No SAE trained and no measure of feature spread across neurons. Dictionary sparsity is assumed from prior work. The Gaussian-control contrast shows non-Gaussian structure but not sparse features.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features not examined.
Theorems use 1-D dictionary directions by assumption; dimensionality is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Toy Models of Superposition only to justify assuming approximate orthogonality. Its Gaussian-control result is compatible with V4 but does not test it: it shows only that structure beyond the second moments matters, not that this structure is sparse dictionary features. Results are figure-only with no uncertainty, and cover one layer per model. Shared-expert, router and learning-rate ablations are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Whether toy networks develop superposed directions, and any sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
The study does not measure feature spread across neurons or recover sparse features using an SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
